::: {.kw-overview}
This issue tracks the immunological and pharmacological threads that decide long-term graft fate, then widens to the donor pool and the operating theatre. A Toronto proteomic study dissects why only some donor-specific-antibody-positive recipients progress to rejection, locating the signal in compartment-specific complement and mitochondrial proteins, while two therapeutic-drug-monitoring papers reframe tacrolimus exposure as both a rejection signal — early underexposure predicting acute rejection — and a cardiometabolic one, with high trough variability tracking post-transplant diabetes. A pragmatic review sets out how to watch for and treat recurrent C3 glomerulopathy when no biomarker yet predicts it. On donor utilisation and infection prevention, the largest cohort yet supports seven-day antiviral prophylaxis to transplant hepatitis-C-viremic donor kidneys into negative recipients, and a Korean cohort shows the recombinant zoster vaccine sharply cutting shingles after transplant. Two final papers speak to donor safety and surgical technique: a 30-year Swiss living-donor registry reassures on kidney function while flagging obese and hypertensive donors, and a single-centre series shows robot-assisted transplantation scaling to deceased-donor and complex cases with low conversion rates.
:::

### 1. [Altered Complement and Tubular Mitochondrial Proteins Are Linked to Graft Loss in DSA+ Antibody-Mediated Rejection](https://doi.org/10.1681/ASN.0000001224)
[Manion KP, Allen MA, Vincent A, Clotet-Freixas S, Pastrello C, Farkona S, Boshart A, Neupane S, Choi HS, Wang S, Huszti E, Su S, Wang J, Kiernan J, Delaney S, Baig S, Famure S, Li Y, Kim SJ, Sarkar A, Jurisica I, John R, Das J, Konvalinka A. *J Am Soc Nephrol*, 2026. PMID: 42593862.]{.kw-ref}

Antibody-mediated rejection is the leading cause of late kidney allograft loss, yet 30–60% of recipients with donor-specific antibodies never develop it, hinting at local tissue adaptations that this study set out to map. The investigators used laser-capture microdissection to separate glomeruli from tubulointerstitium in biopsies from 116 donor-specific-antibody-positive recipients spanning Banff active, chronic active, and mixed antibody-mediated rejection plus a no-rejection group, then ran unbiased mass-spectrometry proteomics and a machine-learning method (SLIDE) to find protein patterns tied to graft loss. They quantified 1,917 glomerular and 2,758 tubulointerstitial proteins, of which 127 and 389 respectively differed significantly across the four groups (one-way ANOVA p<0.05, Tukey FDR<0.05). Chronic active rejection carried the heaviest glomerular signature, dominated by complement and basement-membrane components, and its tubulointerstitial terminal-complement proteins rose independently of C4d staining; mixed rejection instead concentrated its changes in the tubulointerstitium, linked to interferon-γ-driven immune activation, stress responses, and mitochondrial metabolism. Biopsies from antibody-positive recipients without rejection preserved podocyte and tubular proteins but showed none of the conventional accommodation markers. Crucially, SLIDE derived three glomerular and four tubulointerstitial latent factors that separated recipients who lost their grafts from those who did not, correlated with allograft injury, and improved graft-loss prediction beyond standard clinical variables — with complement proteins topping the glomerular model and tubular and mitochondrial proteins the tubulointerstitial one. For UK practice this points toward compartment-resolved molecular signatures that could one day sharpen rejection prognostication beyond DSA titre and C4d, though it remains a discovery-stage tool needing validation.

### 2. [Early Tacrolimus Underexposure Predicts Acute Rejection After Renal Transplantation](https://doi.org/10.1097/FTD.0000000000001516)
[Menke AF, Antony C, Henkel L, Boeckel GR, Houben P, Becker F, Pavenstädt H, Jehn U, Reuter S. *Ther Drug Monit*, 2026. PMID: 42584992.]{.kw-ref}

Tacrolimus combines a narrow therapeutic index with wide pharmacokinetic variability, and while the month-3 concentration-to-dose ratio flags fast metabolisers at higher risk, very early ratios have carried no prognostic weight — leaving a gap this single-centre retrospective study aimed to fill. The authors tested whether early underexposure, defined as trough concentrations below 8 ng/mL during postoperative days 1–10, predicts biopsy-proven acute rejection within 12 months, analysing 374 recipients with complete data for month-3 metabolizer classification and an extended cohort of 609 recipients transplanted between 2007 and 2018 for the rejection analyses. A threshold of 0.29 — the proportion of days 1–10 spent below 8 ng/mL — gave the best balance of sensitivity and specificity, and values above it independently predicted 12-month rejection. Early exposure patterns, however, only modestly discriminated the month-3 metabolizer phenotype, implying that early underexposure and the later concentration-to-dose ratio capture partly distinct risks. The authors position early underexposure as a simple, no-cost metric that complements rather than replaces the established month-3 stratification. Their framing aligns with prior evidence that high early tacrolimus clearance and low exposure raise rejection risk, and argues for tighter attention to target attainment in the first ten days. For UK units, the practical message is that the trough data already collected in the first postoperative week can flag recipients drifting under-immunosuppressed before a rejection episode declares itself, though the retrospective single-centre design limits causal claims.

### 3. [The Association Between Variability in Tacrolimus Trough Levels and Posttransplant Diabetes Mellitus in Thai Kidney Transplant Patients](https://doi.org/10.1097/TXD.0000000000001988)
[Muongmee S, Inkong P, Tasanavipas P, Pongchaidecha M, Nadee C, Mavichak V, Rungprai D. *Transplant Direct*, 2026. PMID: 42592611.]{.kw-ref}

Where the previous paper linked tacrolimus exposure to rejection, this multicentre retrospective study asks whether the *variability* of that exposure drives a different complication — post-transplant diabetes. The authors analysed 516 Thai recipients on twice-daily tacrolimus-based regimens transplanted between 2011 and 2020 (winnowed from 800 assessed for eligibility), calculating the coefficient of variation of trough levels across four windows in the first post-transplant year and diagnosing diabetes by a fasting glucose of at least 126 mg/dL. Post-transplant diabetes developed in 208 patients (40.3%) within that first year, with the cumulative incidence rising steeply in the early months. Higher trough-level variability was significantly associated with diabetes across every interval studied (p<0.001), and receiver-operating-characteristic analysis identified optimal cut-offs of 36% variability at 0–3 and 0–6 months, 23% at 6–12 months, and 33% across 0–12 months. The authors conclude that the coefficient of variation could serve as an accessible marker to flag recipients at high risk of diabetes and prompt closer glycaemic surveillance. The obvious caveats are the single-country, retrospective design, reliance on fasting glucose rather than an oral glucose tolerance test, and the fact that variability may partly reflect adherence or interacting illness rather than a direct diabetogenic mechanism. For UK teams it reinforces intrapatient tacrolimus stability — not just the absolute trough — as a modifiable target worth watching in the metabolically vulnerable.

### 4. [Management of Recurrent C3 Glomerulopathy After Kidney Transplantation](https://doi.org/10.1093/ndt/gfag183)
[Trujillo H, Cavero T, Moran SM, Mirioglu S, Bruchfeld A, Steiger S, Stevens KI, Frangou E, Quintana LF, Kronbichler A, Teng YKO, Praga M, Caravaca-Fontán F. *Nephrol Dial Transplant*, 2026. PMID: 42578942.]{.kw-ref}

C3 glomerulopathy is an ultra-rare disease of alternative-complement-pathway dysregulation with a strong tendency to recur after transplantation, and this practical review distils how to manage that recurrence when the evidence base is thin. The authors emphasise that wider use of protocol biopsies has revealed recurrence to be frequent, often early, and frequently subclinical — histological before it is functional — which reframes it as a surveillance problem rather than one that announces itself. They stress that no validated clinical, genetic, or functional biomarker yet reliably predicts who will recur, and that preventive strategies remain unproven, leading them to favour a pragmatic, monitoring-driven approach over routine prophylaxis. Their framework runs from transplant candidacy and pre-transplant evaluation through post-transplant protocol-biopsy surveillance to therapeutic decision-making, while candidly noting the limits of conventional immunosuppression against a complement-driven process. The emerging role of proximal complement inhibitors is discussed as the most promising therapeutic direction, tempered by uncertainty about when and in whom to deploy them. The authors close on persistent unmet needs: unclear therapeutic goals, how to handle subclinical histological recurrence, and how to interpret treatment response. For UK clinicians counselling patients with C3 glomerulopathy toward transplantation, it offers a coherent, protocol-biopsy-anchored roadmap while being honest that much of the pathway rests on expert opinion rather than trial data.

### 5. [Short Perioperative Antiviral Prophylaxis for Hepatitis C Viremic Donor Kidney Transplantation: Outcomes in 204 Recipients](https://doi.org/10.1097/TP.0000000000005868)
[Dadabaev F, Yakubu I, Agegnehu B, Pontinha V, Moinuddin I, Brown A, Sterling S, Iaria A, Marks R, Sprague T, Kumar D, Seelam SR, Sterling RK, Gupta G. *Transplantation*, 2026. PMID: 42587362.]{.kw-ref}

Transplanting kidneys from hepatitis-C-viremic donors into negative recipients has expanded the usable donor pool in the direct-acting-antiviral era, but real-world data on ultra-short prophylaxis have been scarce, which this single-centre prospective observational study addresses in the largest such cohort to date. It followed 204 consecutive transplants of nucleic-acid-test-positive donor kidneys into hepatitis-C-negative recipients between December 2018 and August 2025, all managed with just seven days of sofosbuvir/velpatasvir 400/100 mg daily begun on the day of transplant, with viral RNA tracked through 90 days and breakthrough triggering full-course therapy. Donor-derived breakthrough viraemia occurred in 15 of 204 recipients (7.4%; 95% CI 4.2–11.9%), almost all detected by postoperative day 28, and NS5A resistance-associated substitutions turned up in four of eight breakthroughs tested. First-line retreatment cleared the virus in 14 of 15, and with one salvage course every breakthrough ultimately achieved sustained virologic response, giving an overall cure rate of 100% — though 93% of retreatments needed insurance prior authorisation, delaying therapy by a median of 36 days. One-year patient and graft survival were 96.6% and 94.1%, with stable function at a mean eGFR of 53.0 ± 22.0 mL/min/1.73 m². On the strength of the resistance substitutions seen, the unit has now switched to seven-day glecaprevir/pibrentasvir. For UK services weighing whether to use hepatitis-C-viremic donors, this supports the feasibility of a short prophylactic course to safely widen the donor pool, with the reimbursement-driven treatment delays being a health-system caveat more than a clinical one.

### 6. [Clinical Effectiveness of the Recombinant Zoster Vaccine for Preventing Herpes Zoster in Individuals With Kidney Transplants: A Retrospective Cohort Study](https://doi.org/10.1111/tid.70300)
[Kwon K, Lim SY, Chang E, Bae S, Kwon H, Jung J, Kim MJ, Shin S, Chong YP, Kim YH, Choi SH, Lee SO, Kim SH. *Transpl Infect Dis*, 2026. PMID: 42583900.]{.kw-ref}

Kidney transplant recipients carry an elevated risk of herpes zoster, and although the recombinant zoster vaccine is recommended for immunocompromised patients on the basis of immunogenicity data, real-world effectiveness evidence in transplant populations has been limited — a gap this retrospective cohort exploited after the vaccine became available in South Korea in March 2023. The study included all 1,761 adults transplanted at a single 2,700-bed tertiary centre in Seoul between January 2020 and December 2024, treating vaccination as a time-varying exposure and using time-dependent Cox regression. Of these, 388 received the vaccine and 1,373 did not; herpes zoster occurred in 78 unvaccinated recipients (5.7%) but in none of the vaccinated group across 398.3 person-years of follow-up. The incidence rate was 16.4 per 1,000 person-years (95% CI 13.0–20.5) among the unvaccinated versus zero (95% CI 0.0–9.3) among the vaccinated, and in a Firth-penalised time-dependent model vaccination was associated with an adjusted hazard ratio of 0.06 (95% CI 0.00–0.43; p<0.001). The authors conclude that the absence of any zoster events after vaccination is consistent with a strong protective effect and supports current recommendations. The zero-event vaccinated arm inevitably produces a wide confidence interval and the retrospective single-centre design invites residual confounding, but the effect size is large. For UK transplant clinics, it adds real-world weight to prioritising recombinant zoster vaccination in kidney transplant recipients.

### 7. [Long Term Outcomes in Living Kidney Donors Over 30 Years](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ekir.2026.106690)
[Krättli J, Buess D, Flohr M, Diebold M, Wehmeier C, Sidler D, Beldi G, Golshayan D, Zingg T, de Seigneux S, Haidar F, Ritter A, Binet I, Hübel K, Rössler F, Steiger J, Hirt-Minkowski P. *Kidney Int Rep*, 2026. PMID: 42569397.]{.kw-ref}

Living donation offers recipients major benefits, but the long-term safety of the donor remains the ethical linchpin, and this prospective cohort brings unusually long follow-up from the Swiss Organ Living-Donor Health Registry — established in 1993 as the world's first such registry. The analysis included 1,863 donors who gave a kidney between 1993 and 2018 and had at least five years of follow-up, tracked until death, kidney failure, or last visit with censoring at 31 March 2024, using linear mixed-effects models for eGFR trajectories from 12 months onward. Donors had a median age of 53 years, were 66.2% female, and 15.5% had treated hypertension before donation, with a median predonation eGFR of 96 mL/min/1.73 m² and a median follow-up of 12 years (IQR 7–18). Reassuringly, kidney function was essentially stable, with a mean annual eGFR change of +0.14 mL/min/1.73 m², though slopes were flatter — that is, less favourable — in obese and hypertensive donors and more stable in women and non-obese, non-hypertensive donors. Hard outcomes were rare: three donors (0.2%) reached dialysis-dependent kidney failure, 17 (0.9%) an eGFR below 30, 28 (1.5%) persistent severe proteinuria, and 40 (2.1%) the composite endpoint, which was independently predicted by male sex, older age, and predonation obesity. The authors read this as broadly reassuring while arguing for standardised lifelong surveillance. For UK donor programmes it supports current practice and sharpens counselling for obese or hypertensive candidates, in whom trajectories were measurably less benign.

### 8. [Robot-assisted kidney transplantation in living and deceased donors: a six-year experience](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11701-026-03773-z)
[Siddiqui HU, Isaacson D, Shoucair S, Wu W, Krishnamurthi V, Lin YC, Wee A, Kaouk J, Eltemamy M. *J Robot Surg*, 2026. PMID: 42579218.]{.kw-ref}

Robot-assisted kidney transplantation has spread quickly, but most reported series are dominated by living-donor cases, leaving its performance in deceased-donor and complex transplants under-described — the gap this single-centre study fills from a prospectively maintained registry spanning October 2019 to December 2025. Across 228 recipients, 125 (54.8%) received deceased-donor and 103 (45.2%) living-donor kidneys, with single-port and multiport robotic platforms used in 30.7% and 69.3% of cases respectively, alongside six dual-kidney and four simultaneous kidney-pancreas procedures; annual volume climbed from a single case in 2019 to 115 in 2025. Median operative time was 3 hours 38 minutes for deceased-donor and 4 hours 6 minutes for living-donor transplants, with vascular anastomosis times of 44 and 40 minutes and a median estimated blood loss of just 50 mL in both groups. Conversion to open surgery occurred in only one patient (0.4%), and median length of stay was four days for deceased-donor and two days for living-donor recipients. Delayed graft function affected 30.4% of deceased-donor recipients (whose grafts carried a median Kidney Donor Profile Index of 55% and cold ischaemia of about 21 hours) versus 4.8% of living-donor recipients, and among the 121 with one-year data median serum creatinine was 1.49 and 1.37 mg/dL respectively. Graft loss (1.6% deceased-donor, 0.9% living-donor) and mortality (2.4% and 0.9%) were low despite rising case complexity. For UK centres contemplating or expanding robotic transplant programmes, this is encouraging evidence that the approach scales to deceased-donor and complex work with a very low conversion rate, albeit from a single high-volume team without a randomised comparator.
